pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Acute Thallium Poisoning (Thallotoxicosis) THE SMOKING GUN: The classic clinical triad of acute gastrointestinal distress, excruciating painful peripheral neuropathy (hyperpathia/allodynia mimicking GBS), followed by rapid, delayed alopecia (anagen effluvium) and Mees lines on the nails. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Thallium (Tl+) shares an identical ionic radius and charge to Potassium (K+), enabling it to substitute for potassium across biological membranes via the Na+/K+-ATPase pump. Once intracellular, thallium exhibits a high affinity for sulfhydryl (-SH) groups on vital mitochondrial proteins, notably inhibiting pyruvate kinase, succinate dehydrogenase, and the electron transport chain. This causes catastrophic ATP depletion and lipid peroxidation. Tissues with the highest metabolic demands are preferentially destroyed: long axons suffer severe dying-back axonal degeneration (causing relentless neuropathic pain and weakness), while fast-dividing keratinocytes in hair follicles undergo immediate mitotic arrest, leading to hallmark whole-scalp alopecia within 2 to 3 weeks of exposure.
